title: Wireless Doorbell
pitch: Press a button at the door and a second board inside plays a chime, over a cheap 433MHz radio link.

guide.about: One board sends a secret number when the button is pressed; the other listens and plays a ding-dong when it hears that exact number. One sketch does both jobs: set IS_SENDER.
parts: or a nice metal doorbell button
wiring: must be Pin 2: it uses an interrupt
solder a straight 17 cm wire for much better range
steps: Install the rc-switch library.
Solder a 17 cm straight wire to the ANT hole of each module (optional but recommended).
Sender board: wire the transmitter (DATA → Pin 10) and the button (Pin 4). Set IS_SENDER = true and upload.
Receiver board: wire the receiver (DATA → Pin 2) and buzzer (Pin 8). Set IS_SENDER = false and upload.
Open the receiver's Serial Monitor (9600) and press the button.
guide.test: Each press makes the receiver print "Doorbell code received" and play a two-tone chime. Other 433MHz remotes nearby are ignored because they send different numbers.
safety: Soldering the antenna wires: hot iron, use the stand and ventilate.
next: Use the RXB6 receiver for longer range.
Add a second button with a different code for the back door.

title: Water Leak Alarm
pitch: Place the sensor under the sink or washing machine: a drop of water triggers a loud alarm.

guide.about: The sensor's metal traces conduct when wet. To stop them corroding, the board powers the sensor from a pin for just a moment every 2 seconds.
parts: or the FC-37 rain plate (use its AO pin)
long wires to reach the floor
steps: Wire the sensor's + to Pin 7 (not 5V!), − to GND and S to A0.
Wire the buzzer through 220Ω to Pin 8.
Upload and open the Serial Monitor at 9600: dry readings should be near 0.
Touch the sensor with a wet finger: the reading jumps and the alarm sounds.
Lay the sensor flat on the floor where a leak would start, with the board up high and dry.
guide.test: Dry: quiet. Wet (reading above WET_LEVEL): siren beeps and the LED flashes until it's dry again.
safety: Keep the board and USB charger high and dry: only the sensor goes on the floor.
next: Use an ESP32 to send a phone alert (see Motion Alert to your iPhone).
Add a second sensor near the water heater.

title: Flame Spotter (demo)
pitch: Detects the flicker of a candle flame and sounds an alarm: a fun science demo about infrared light.

guide.about: Flames give off infrared light that this sensor is tuned to. Its DO pin says "flame / no flame" and AO shows how strong it is.
steps: Wire the sensor: VCC 5V, GND, DO Pin 2, AO A0.
Wire the buzzer (Pin 8 via 220Ω) and the optional LED (Pin 13).
Upload and open the Serial Monitor at 9600.
Have an adult light a candle about 50 cm away. Turn the sensor's screw until its DO light turns ON with the flame and OFF without it.
guide.test: With the flame in view: beeping and the LED blinks. Blow out the candle and it goes quiet.
safety: Only with an adult present. Keep the candle on a non-flammable surface, away from wires and the breadboard.
This is NOT a fire alarm. Never rely on it for safety.
next: Mount it on a servo to scan the room.
Show the flame strength as a bar on an LCD.

title: Event Countdown (Eid, birthday…)
pitch: Shows how many days are left until a special day. Set your date, and it counts down by itself.

guide.about: The DS3231 knows today's date; the code subtracts it from your target date. A button shows hours instead of days. On the big day the display flashes.
steps: Install RTClib and TM1637.
Put your event's date into TARGET_YEAR, TARGET_MONTH and TARGET_DAY.
Wire the DS3231 (A4/A5) and the TM1637 (pins 3/4).
Upload. The clock takes your PC's time the first time.
Hold the button to see the hours left.
guide.test: The display shows the days left (e.g. 42). On the day itself it flashes 0000. After the day it shows dashes.
next: Decorate it as a gift for a friend's birthday.
Add a buzzer that plays a tune at midnight on the day.

title: Party Sound Meter
pitch: A rainbow LED bar that jumps with the music: green when calm, red when the party gets loud.

guide.about: The code samples the microphone hundreds of times per frame and measures the swing (peak-to-peak) to get loudness, then lights that many LEDs with a falling peak dot.
parts: or MAX4466 / MAX9814 (use its OUT pin)
steps: Install Adafruit NeoPixel.
Wire the microphone's analog output to A0 (5V and GND too).
Wire the LED stick: 5V, GND, DIN through 330Ω to Pin 6.
Upload, play some music and clap!
If it's too jumpy or too calm, change SENSITIVITY in the code.
guide.test: Silence shows nothing or one green LED. Talking lights a few, music fills the bar toward red, and a white dot marks the recent peak.
next: Use a 16-LED ring for a circular VU meter.
Mirror the bar from the center outward.

title: Board Game Score Keeper
pitch: Turn a knob to add or remove points, click to switch player. Never argue about the score again!

guide.about: A rotary encoder sends two signals slightly out of step; their order tells the direction. The display shows the player number and their score.
parts: or a power bank on the game table
steps: Install the TM1637 library.
Wire the encoder (CLK 2, DT 3, SW 4) and the display (CLK 5, DIO 6).
Upload.
Turn the knob to change the score; click to switch between players 1–4; hold 3 s to reset all scores.
guide.test: The display shows e.g. "2 15": player 2 has 15 points. Each click of the knob is exactly one point.
next: Show all players' scores in turn on a 20x4 LCD.
Add a buzzer when someone reaches the winning score.

title: Light Harp
pitch: Wave your hand over a light sensor to play spooky sliding notes, like a magic instrument.

guide.about: The code measures the room light for 3 seconds at startup. When your hand casts a shadow, the darker it gets, the higher the note.
steps: Build the light divider: LDR from 5V to A0, 10kΩ from A0 to GND.
Wire the buzzer through 220Ω to Pin 8.
Upload and keep your hand away for 3 seconds (calibration).
Move your hand above the sensor to play.
guide.test: No shadow = silence. A light shadow plays low notes; covering it fully plays high notes.
next: Snap notes to a musical scale (see the theremin idea).
Use two LDRs for two "strings".

title: Ultrasonic Theremin
pitch: Play music in the air: move your hand closer or farther from the sensor to change the note.

guide.about: Distance becomes pitch. The notes snap to a pentatonic scale (5 notes that always sound nice together), so anything you play sounds musical.
steps: Wire the sensor (TRIG 7, ECHO 6) and the buzzer (Pin 8 through 220Ω).
Upload.
Hold your hand 5–50 cm above the sensor and move it slowly up and down.
guide.test: Close = high notes, far = low notes. Beyond 50 cm it's silent. Set SMOOTH = true for sliding sci-fi sounds instead of notes.
next: Add a button to switch scales.
Add a light sensor for volume (sort of) by changing note length.

title: Binary Counter Trainer
pitch: Four LEDs count from 0 to 15 in binary as you press a button: learn how computers count.

guide.about: Each LED is a "bit": worth 1, 2, 4 and 8. Add up the lit ones and you get the number. The Serial Monitor shows the decimal and binary side by side.
steps: Place 4 LEDs in a row, rightmost = 1, then 2, 4, 8 going left.
Wire each with a 220Ω resistor to pins 2, 3, 4, 5 (right to left).
Wire the button between Pin 7 and GND.
Upload, open the Serial Monitor (9600) and press the button.
guide.test: Each press adds 1: 0001, 0010, 0011… up to 1111 (15), then back to 0. Hold the button 1 second to reset.
next: Add a 5th LED (16) to count to 31.
Quiz mode: show a number in binary and guess it.

title: Kitchen Scale
pitch: Build a digital scale that weighs up to 5 kg in grams, with tare (zero) and an LCD readout.

guide.about: A load cell bends a tiny bit under weight; the HX711 measures that tiny change. The code reads the HX711 directly (no extra library), subtracts the empty weight (tare) and converts to grams with a calibration factor you find once.
parts: plus two small boards/plates and screws for mounting
steps: Mount the load cell like a Z: one end screwed to a base plate, the other end to the top plate (the arrow on the cell points down).
Wire the load cell to the HX711, then the HX711 to the board (DT 3, SCK 2).
Install LiquidCrystal I2C, wire the LCD, and upload.
With nothing on the scale, it zeroes itself at startup.
Calibrate: put something of known weight (e.g. a 500 g pack) on it. The Serial Monitor (9600) shows the raw value; set CALIBRATION = raw value ÷ grams, upload again.
guide.test: Empty shows 0 g. Your known weight shows its correct weight within a few grams. Press TARE with a bowl on it to zero the bowl.
safety: Don't overload the cell beyond 5 kg: it can bend permanently.
next: Add a buzzer that beeps at a target weight (great for coffee!).
Show ounces with a second button.

title: IR Remote Copier
pitch: Teach it any button from your TV remote, then press its own button to send that code. A DIY universal remote!

guide.about: The IR receiver captures a remote's code; the infrared LED sends it back out. Hold the button to learn, tap it to send. Works with most TV remotes; some air-conditioner remotes use codes too long to copy.
wiring: through 220Ω (Pin 3 is fixed by the IR library)
steps: Install the IRremote library.
Wire the receiver (OUT → Pin 2), the IR LED with 220Ω on Pin 3, and the button on Pin 4.
Upload and open the Serial Monitor at 9600.
Hold the button for 2 seconds until it says LEARNING, then press a button on your TV remote.
Point the IR LED at the TV and tap the button: the TV reacts!
guide.test: Learned codes print as e.g. "Learned NEC address 0x4 command 0x8". Tapping sends it. Tip: look at the IR LED through your phone camera to see it flash.
next: Learn 4 buttons with 4 push buttons.
Add a transistor for more range (several metres).
